GENERAL OBJECTIONS TO PUBLIC RELIEF AND TO PRIVATE ALMS-GIVING. The fact was adverted to in the beginning of this article, that the state of the

POOR-LAWS

Pages 318-319

poor-laws have not diminished the capital, but rather the rent of the landlord, as the tenant considers rents and rates as payment for the farm, and one can only be increased at the expense of the other." "The farmers are aware that, excepting in cases of great tenants and very sudden augmentation of rates, the burden does not at all affect them. It is a rent paid to the parish instead of the landowner." "It should be understood that poor-rates are deducted in all calculations for rent; and that landlords pay them, and not the farmers." "Capital is decreasing, from the loose manner in which the laws are administered, and the tenants feeling that they do not in effect pay the rates, but the landlord. I cannot otherwise account for the apathy with which they view, and the tenacity with which, in many instances, they defend abuses." (Report, pp. 60, 61, 62.)

POPAYAN

Pages 328-329

a town of New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the department of Cauca, stands near the source of the river Cauca, at an elevation of 5824 feet above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, 230 miles S.W. of Bogota. It is regularly laid out and well built, consisting for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of brick houses one storey <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Of its many squares, one is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome. The town contains a university, a Jesuit <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, and several other churches and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, besides other public buildings. Popayan has declined considerably from its former condition, both in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> and commercial importance. There was at one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> a considerable trade in the precious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-METALS">metals</a> carried on here; but since the revolution these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> have been conveyed by different channels, and there is now at Popayan only some little traffic in woollen fabrics, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and agricultural produce. This was the earliest town built by Europeans in this part of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, having been founded by Benalcazar in 1537.

POPE

Pages 329-347

a name which comes from the Greek word Πάπας, and signifies Father. In the East this appellation is given to all Christian priests, and in the West <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> were called by it in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times; but since the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Gregory VII. it has been appropriated to the Bishop of Rome, whom the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> look upon as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> father of all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Within the last two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> three centuries much has been said and written, and many warm disputes have been carried on, concerning the Pope, and the power belonging to him. All those in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the see of Rome unanimously hold that our Saviour <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ constituted St <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> pastor under himself, to watch over his whole flock here upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and to preserve the unity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, at the same time giving him the power requisite for these ends. They also believe that our Saviour ordained that St Peter should have successors with the like authority and power to the end of time. Now, as they allege that St Peter resided for many years at Rome, and there suffered martyrdom, they consider the bishops of Rome as his successors in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and office of the universal pastor of the whole Catholic church. There have been some varieties in the manner of choosing the bishop of Rome in different ages, as alterations may be made in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; but still the clergy of Rome have always had the chief <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>; and that clergy is now represented by, or in some manner consists of the cardinals, who have for several centuries been the sole electors of the Pope. These cardinals, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons of the Church of Rome, are seventy in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, when the Sacred <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, as it is called, is complete. Of these, six are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> bishops,—viz., the bishops of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OSTIA">Ostia</a>, Porto, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a>, Sabino, Tusculum or Frascati, and Praneste or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PALESTRINA">Palestrina</a>, which are the six suburbicarian churches; fifty are cardinal priests, who have all titles from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches in Rome; and fourteen are cardinal deacons, who have their titles from churches in Rome of less <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, called diaconias or deaconries. These cardinals are created by the Pope when there happen to be vacancies. Sometimes he names one or two only at a time; but <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> he defers the promotion until there be ten or twelve vacancies or more; and then at every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> promotion, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, the kings of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and France, and of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> when Catholic, are allowed to present one each, to be made cardinal, whom the Pope always admits <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be not some very great and evident objection. These cardinals are commonly promoted from amongst such clergymen as have borne offices in the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>; some are assumed from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> orders; and eminent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> of other countries are likewise often honoured with this dignity. Sons of sovereign princes have frequently been members of the sacred college. Their distinctive dress is scarlet, to signify that they ought to be ready to shed their blood for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and the church, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of either require it. They wear a scarlet <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> and hat. The cap is given to them by the Pope if they are at Rome, and is sent to them if they are absent; but the hat is never given but by the Pope's own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. These cardinals form the Pope's standing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> or consistory for the management of the public affairs of church and state. They are divided into different congregations, for the more easy despatch of business; and some of them hold the principal offices in the pontifical court,—as that of cardinal-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENITENTIARY">penitentiary</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, camerlingo or chamberlain, prefect of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, prefect of memorials, and secretary of state. They have the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of eminence and most eminent given them. But here we consider them principally as the persons entrusted with the choice of the Pope. On the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a> of a Pope, his pontifical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> is immediately broken by the chamberlain, and all public business is interrupted that can be delayed. Messengers are despatched to all the Catholic sovereigns to acquaint them of the event, that they may take what <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> they think proper, and that the cardinals in their dominions, if any there be, may hasten to the future election if they choose to attend; whilst the whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the sacred college is turned to the preservation of tranquillity in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and state, and to the necessary preparations for the future election. The cardinal chamberlain, during the vacancy of the Holy See, possesses great authority; he coins <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a> with his own arms on it, lodges in the Pope's apartments, and is attended by bodyguards. He, and the first cardinal bishop, the first cardinal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and the first cardinal deacon, have during that time the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> almost entirely in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The body of the deceased Pope is carried to St Peter's, where funeral <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is performed for him with great pomp during <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days, and the cardinals attend there every morning. In the meantime, all necessary preparations for the election are made; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they assemble for that purpose, which is called the conclave, is fitted up in that part of the Vatican <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> which is nearest St Peter's church, as this has <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been thought the most convenient situation. Here is formed by partitions of wood a number of cells or chambers equal to the number of cardinals, with a small distance between every two, and a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> gallery before them. A number is put upon every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, and small papers with corresponding numbers are put into a box. Every cardinal, or some one for him, draws out one of these papers, which determines in what cell he is to lodge. The cells are lined with cloth; and there is a part of each one separated for the conclavists or attendants, of whom two are allowed to each cardinal, and three to cardinal princes. They are persons of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and generally of great confidence; but they must carry in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s meals, serve him at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and perform all the offices of a menial <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>. Two physicians, two surgeons, an apothecary, and some other necessary officers, are chosen for the conclave by the cardinals. On the tenth <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the Pope's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the cardinals who are then in Rome, and in a competent state of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, meet in the chapel of St Peter's, which is called the Gregorian Chapel, where a sermon on the choice of a Pope is preached to them, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> is said for invoking the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of the Holy Ghost. Then the cardinals proceed to the conclave in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> two by two, and take up their abode. When all is properly settled, the conclave is shut up, having boxed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> or places of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> in convenient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>; and there are also strong guards placed all around. When any foreign cardinal arrives after the inclosure, the conclave is opened for his admission. In the beginning every cardinal signs a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, containing an obligation that if he shall be raised to the papal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> he <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> not alienate any part of the pontifical dominion; that he will not be prodigal to his relations; and such other stipulations as may have been settled in former times or framed for the occasion. We come now to the election itself; and that this may be effectual, two-thirds of the cardinals present must vote for the same person. As this is often not easily obtained, they sometimes remain whole months in the conclave. They meet in the chapel twice every day for giving their votes; and the election may be effected by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCRUTINY">scrutiny</a>, accession, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACCLAMATION">acclamation</a>. Scrutiny is the ordinary method, and consists in this: every cardinal writes his own name on the inner part of a piece of paper, and this is folded up and sealed. On a second fold of the same paper a conclave writes the name of the person for whom his master votes. This, according to the practice observed for some centuries, must be one of the Sacred College. On the outer side of the paper is written a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> at random, which the voter must well remember. Every cardinal, on entering into the chapel, goes to the altar and puts his paper into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> chalice. When all are convened, two cardinals number the votes; and if they are more or less than the number of cardinals present the voting must be repeated. When that is not the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the cardinal appointed for the purpose reads the outer sentence, and the name of the cardinal under it, so that each voter hearing his own sentence and the name joined with it, knows that there is no mistake. The names of all the cardinals that are voted for are taken <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, with the number of votes for each; and when it appears that any has two-thirds of the number present in his favour the election is over; but when this does not happen, the voting papers are all immediately burned without opening up the inner part. When several trials of coming to a conclusion by this method of scrutiny have been made in vain, recourse is sometimes had to what is called accession. By it, when a cardinal perceives that one or very few votes are wanting to any one for whom he had not voted at that time, he may say that he accedes to the one who has nearly the number of votes requisite; and if his one vote suffices to make up the two-thirds, or if he is followed by a sufficient number of new voters for the said cardinal, the election is accomplished. Lastly, a Pope is sometimes elected by acclamation; that is, when a cardinal, being pretty sure that he will be joined by a sufficient number, cries out in the open chapel that such a one shall be Pope. If he is supported properly, the election becomes unanimous,—those who would perhaps oppose it foreseeing that their opposition would be fruitless, and rather hurtful to themselves. It is to be observed that the emperor of Germany and the kings of France and Spain claimed a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of excluding one cardinal from being Pope at every election. Hence, when the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> at Rome of any of these sovereigns perceived that any cardinal disagreeable to his master was likely to be made Pope, he demanded an audience of the conclave, was admitted, and there declared his master's will, which was always attended to for the common good. But each of those sovereigns was thus allowed to exclude only one at a time, and they unwillingly and seldom put this right in execution. When a Pope is chosen in any of the three above-mentioned ways, the election is immediately announced from the balcony in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of St Peter's; homage is paid to the new pontiff; and couriers are sent off with the news to all parts of Christendom. The Pope appoints a day for his coronation at St Peter's, and for his taking possession of the patriarchal church of St John Lateran, all which is performed with great solemnity. He is addressed by the title of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOLINESS">Holiness</a>, and Most Holy Father. Let us now proceed to state what authority Roman Catholics <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to the Pope thus chosen. They believe, then, that the Bishop of Rome is, under Christ, supreme pastor of the whole church; and, as such, is not only the first bishop in order and dignity, but has also a power and jurisdiction over all Christians, to preserve unity and purity of faith and moral doctrine, and to maintain order and regularity in all churches. Wherefore they hold, that when the Pope understands that any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> has been broached against faith or manners, or that any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> on such subjects has arisen in any part of Christendom, it belongs to him, after due deliberation and consultation, to issue out his pastoral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, condemning the error, clearing up the doubt, and declaring what has been handed down, and what is to be believed. Some Catholic divines are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the Pope cannot err when he thus addresses himself to all the faithful on matters of doctrine. They well know that as a private <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> he may <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into mistakes as well as any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>; but they think that when he teaches the whole church <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> must preserve him from error; and they apprehend that this may be deduced from the promises of Christ to St Peter, and from the writings of the ancient fathers. It is to be observed, however, that this infallibility of the Pope, even when he pronounces in the most solemn manner, is only an opinion, and not an article of Roman Catholic faith. Wherefore, when he sends forth doctrinal decrees, the other bishops, who are also guardians of the faith in an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, may, with due respect, examine these decrees; and if they find them agree with what has always been taught, they either formally signify their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a>, or they tacitly acquiesce, which, considering their duty, is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a formal approbation. When the acceptation of the generality of the bishops has been obtained, either immediately or after some mutual correspondence and explanation, the decrees of the Pope thus accepted come to be the sentence of the whole church, and are believed to be beyond the possibility of error. Sometimes it happens that the disputes and differences may be so great and intricate that, to the end it may be seen more clearly what has really been delivered down, and to give all possible satisfaction, it may appear proper to convene all the bishops who can conveniently attend at one place, to learn from them more distinctly what has been taught and held in their respective churches. Roman Catholics believe that it belongs to the Pope to call such general councils, and to preside in them in person, or by his legates. They likewise hold, that when the Pope has approved the decrees of such councils concerning faith or manners, such decrees become <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a>, and must be received as such by all Catholics. In all this they believe that the particular assistance of the Holy Ghost is with the pastors of the church, and that therefore "the gates of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELL">hell</a> shall not prevail against it." The see of Rome, according to the Roman Catholics, is the centre of Catholic unity. All their bishops communicate with the Pope, and by his means with one another, and so form one body. However distant their particular churches may be, they all meet at Rome either in person or by their delegates, or at least by their letters; and, according to the discipline of the latter ages, though they are presented to the Pope for their office from their respective countries, yet from him they must receive their bulls of consecration before they can take possession of their sees. In matters of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> discipline the Pope, as chief pastor, not only must take care that the canons actually in force be observed in all churches, but he may also make new canons and regulations when he sees it necessary or expedient for the spiritual benefit of the faithful, according to times and circumstances. France | 1316 | | Benedict XII | of France | 1334 | | Clement VI | French | 1342 | Pope, Alexander, the most brilliant of all wits who have at any time applied themselves to the poetic treatment of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> manners, to the selecting from the play of human character what is picturesque, or the arresting what is fugitive, was born in the city of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> on the 21st day of May in the memorable year 1688; about six months, therefore, before the landing of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and the opening of that great revolution which gave the final ratification to all previous revolutions of that tempestuous century. By the "city" of London the reader is to understand us as speaking with technical accuracy of that district which lies within the ancient walls and the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor. The parents of Pope, there is good reason to think, were of "gentle blood," which is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the poet himself when describing them in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. His mother was so undoubtedly; and her illustrious son, in speaking of her to Lord Hervey at a time when any exaggeration was open to an easy refutation, and writing in a spirit most likely to provoke it, does not scruple to say, with a tone of dignified haughtiness not unbecoming the situation of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> champion on behalf of an insulted mother, that by birth and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> she was not below that young lady (one of the two beautiful Miss Lepels) whom his lordship had selected from all the choir of court beauties as the future mother of his children. Of Pope's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> and immediate lineage for a space of two generations we know enough; beyond that we know little; of this little a part is dubious; and what we are disposed to receive as not dubious rests chiefly on his own authority. In the prologue to his Satires, having occasion to notice the lampooners of the times, who had represented his father as "a mechanic, a hatter, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, nay, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BANKRUPT">bankrupt</a>," he feels himself called upon to state the --- 1 This interesting memoir of Pope was contributed to the previous edition of the Encyclopaedia by Mr De Quincey. It is retained in the present edition, as presenting a valuable critical estimate and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of a great English classic, by one of the most acute and scholastic writers of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. It has been found necessary, however, to make a few additions (included within brackets) embodying the results of some of the recent investigations into the history of Pope. 2 Dr Johnson, however, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Warton, for reasons not stated, have placed his birth on the 22d. To this statement, as opposed to that which comes from the personal friends of Pope, little attention is due. Ruffhead and Spence, upon such questions, must always be of higher authority than Johnson and Warton, and d'Herbelot than Bowles. But it ought not to be concealed, though hitherto unnoticed by any person, that some doubt as to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of Pope's birth remains whether any of the biographers is right. An anonymous writer, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Pope, and evidently familiar with his personal history, declares that he was born on the 8th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>; and he connects it with an event that, having a public and a partisan <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> (the birth of that Prince of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> who was known twenty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years afterwards as the Pretender), would serve to check his own recollections, and give them a national tinge. It is true he wrote for an ill-natured purpose; but no purpose whatever could have been prompted by the falsification of the particular date. What is still more noticeable, however, Pope himself puts a most emphatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> upon all these statements. In a pathetic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to a friend, when his attention could not have been wandering, for he is expressly insisting upon a sentiment which will find an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECHO">echo</a> in many a human heart, viz., that a birthday, though from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> usually celebrated as a festal day, too often is secretly a memorial of disappointment, and an anniversary of sorrowful memories. He speaks of the very day on which he is then writing as his own birthday; and indeed what else could give any propriety to the passage? Now the date of this letter is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1, 1733. Surely Pope knew his own birthday better than those who have adopted a random rumour without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. [Mr De Quincey's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> has here misled him; no date is affixed by Pope to this letter. Allusion is made in it to the death of Congreve as a very recent occurrence; and as Congreve died on the 19th of January 1729, it may be inferred that Pope's birthday was near the time of Congreve's decease, in the latter end of January or beginning of February. But in preparing his letters for the press, Pope altered and revised them; sometimes making one printed epistle out of two or more written ones, and little or no reliance can be placed on the poet's dates.] But, whilst we are upon this subject, we must caution the readers of Pope against too much reliance upon the chronological accuracy of his editors. All are scandalously careless; and generally they are faithless. Many important dates are left unnoticed, which a very little research would have illustrated; many facts are omitted, even yet recoverable, which are essential to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> appreciation of Pope's satirical blows; and dates are constantly mistated. Mr Ramsay, the most careful of Pope's editors; but even he is often wrong. For instance, he has taken the trouble to write a note upon Pope's famous report to Lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> journey on horseback with Lintot; and this note involves a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> impossibility. The letter is undated, except as to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; and Mr Roscoe directs the reader to supply 1714 as the true date, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> anachronism. For a ludicrous anecdote is there put into Lintot's mouth, representing some angry critic, who had been <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> over Pope's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> with frequent pauses, as having been prophesied, by Mr Lintot's dinner, into a gentler feeling towards Pope, and finally, by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> effect of good cheer, without an effort on the publisher's part, as coming to a confession, that what he ate and what he had been <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a> were equally excellent. But in the year 1714, no part <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> about his parents; and naturally much more so at a time when the low scurrilities of these obscure libellers had been adopted, accredited, and diffused by persons so distinguished in all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of personal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> and rank as Lady <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Wortley Montagu and Lord Hervey: "hard as thy heart," was one of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASQUINADE">pasquinade</a>, "hard as thy heart, and as thy birth obscure." Accordingly he makes the following formal statement:—"Mr Pope's father was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s family in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, the head of which was the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Downe. His mother was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of William Turner, Esq., of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a>; she had three brothers, one of whom was killed; another died in the service of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> [meaning Charles I.]; the eldest, following his fortunes, and becoming a general officer in Spain, left her what estate remained after the sequestrations and forfeitures of her family." The sequestrations here spoken of were those inflicted by the commissioners for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>; and usually they levied a fifth, or even two-fifths, according to the apparent delinquency of the parties. But in such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> two great differences arose in the treatment of the royalists; first, that the report was coloured according to the interest which a man possessed, or other private means for biasing the commissioners; secondly, that often, when money could not be raised on mortgage to meet the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEQUESTRATION">sequestration</a>, it became necessary to sell a family estate suddenly, and therefore in those times at great loss; so that a nominal fifth might be depressed by favour to a tenth, or raised by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of selling to a half. And hence might arise the small dowry of Mrs Pope, notwithstanding the family estate in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> had centred in her person. But, by the way, we see from the fact of the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> having sought service in Spain, that Mrs Pope was a Papist; not, like her husband, by conversion, but by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> faith. This account, as publicly thrown out in the way of challenge by Pope, was, however, sneered at by a certain Mr Pottinger of those days, who, together with his absurd name, has been safely transmitted to posterity in connection with this single fear of having contradicted Alexander Pope. We read in a diary published by the Microcosm, "Met a large hat with a man under it." And so, here, we cannot so properly say that Mr Pottinger brings down the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to our times, as that the contradiction brings down Mr Pottinger. "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUSIN">Cousin</a> Pope," said Pottinger, "had made himself out a fine pedigree, but he wondered where he got it;" and he then goes on to plead in abatement of Pope's pretensions, "that an old maiden aunt, equally related" (that is, standing in the same relation to himself and to the poet), "a great genealogist, who was always talking of her family, never mentioned this circumstance." And again we are told, from another <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, that the Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUILDFORD">Guildford</a>, after express investigation of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, "was sure that," amongst the descendants of the Earls of Downe, "there was none of the name of Pope." How it was that Lord Guildford came to have any connection with the affair, is of Pope's Homer was printed. June 1715 was the month in which even the subscribers first received the four earliest books of the Iliad, and the public generally not until <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. This we notice by way of specimen. In itself, or as an error of mere negligence, it would be of little importance; but it is a case to which Mr Roscoe has expressly applied his own conjectural skill, and solicited the attention of his reader. We may judge, therefore, of his accuracy in other cases which he did not think worthy of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>. [The letter contains a reference to Lord Lansdowne's committal to the Tower, which serves to fix the date between September 1715 and February 1716, when he was released.] There is another instance, presenting itself in every page, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> concurring with laxness on the part of all Pope's editors, and with the effect not so purely of misleading as of perplexing the general reader. Until Lord Macclesfield's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BILL">bill</a> for altering the style in the very middle of the eighteenth century, it was therefore after the death of Pope, there was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, arising from the collision between the civil and ecclesiastical year, of dating the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> that lies between <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 31st and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 25th (both days exclusively) as belonging indifferently to the past or the current year. This peculiarity had nothing to do with the old and new style, but was, we believe, redressed by the same <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of Parliament. Now in Pope's time it was absolutely necessary that a man should <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> date, because else he was liable to be seriously misunderstood. For instance, it was then always said that Charles I. had suffered on the 30th of January 1649; and why? Because, had the historian fixed the date to what it really was, 1649, in that case all those (a very numerous class) who supposed the year 1649 to commence on Ladyday, or March 25, would have understood him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that this event happened in what we now call 1650, for not until 1650 was there any January which they would have acknowledged as belonging to 1649, since they added to the year 1648 all the days from January 1 to March 24. On the other hand, if he had said simply that Charles suffered in 1648, he would have been truly understood by the class we have just mentioned; but by another class, who began the year from the 1st of January, he would have been understood to mean what we now mean by the year 1648. There would have been a sheer difference, not of one, as the reader might think at first sight, but of two entire years in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of the two parties; which difference, and all possibility of doubt, is met and remedied by the fractional date 1648: for that date says in effect it was 1648 to you who do not open the new year till Ladyday; it was 1649 to you who open it from January 1. Thus much to explain the real <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the case; and it follows from this explanation, that no part of the year ever can have fractional or double date except the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> from January 1 to March 24 inclusively. And hence arises a practical inconvenience, viz., that the same reason, and no other, which formerly enjoined the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> or fractional date,—viz., the prevention of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> ambiguity or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DILEMMA">dilemma</a>, now enjoins its omission. For in our day, when the double opening of the year is abolished, what sense is there in perplexing a reader by using a fraction which offers him a choice without directing him how to choose. In fact, it is the denominator of the fraction, if one may so style the lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, which expresses to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> eye the true year. Yet the editors of Pope, as well as many other writers, have confused their readers by this double date; and why? Simply because they were confused themselves. Many errors in literature of large <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> have arisen from this confusion. Thus it was said properly enough in the contemporary accounts—for instance, in Lord Monmouth's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>—that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> died on the last day of the year 1602, for she died on the 24th of March; and by a careful writer this event would have been dated as March 24, 1602. But many writers, misled by the phrase above cited, have asserted that James I. was proclaimed on the 1st of January 1603. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a>, Bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>, again, has ruined the entire chronology of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Jeremy Taylor, and unconsciously vitiated the facts, by not understanding this fractional date. Mr Roscoe even too often leaves his readers to collect the true year as they can: thus, e.g., at p. 500 of his Life, he quotes from Pope's letter to Warburton, in great vexation for the surreptitious publication of his letters in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, under date of February 4, 1741. But why not have printed it intelligibly as 1741? Incidents there are in most men's lives which are susceptible of a totally different moral value, according as they are dated in one year or another. That might be a kind and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> liberality in 1740 which would be a fraud upon creditors in 1741. Exile to a distance of 10 miles from London in January 1744, might argue that a man was a turbulent citizen and suspected of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; whilst the same exile in January 1745 would simply argue that, as a Papist, he had been included amongst his whole body in a general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of precaution to meet the public dangers of that year. This explanation we have thought it right to make, both for its extensive application to all editions of Pope, and on account of the serious blunders which have arisen from the case when ill understood; and because, in a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, written jointly by Messrs Lant Carpenter and Sheppard, though generally men of ability and learning, this whole point is erroneously explained. VOL. XVIII. not stated by the biographers of Pope; but we have ascertained that, by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> descendant from the Earls of Downe, he had come into possession of their English estates. Finally, though it is rather for the honour of the Earls of Downe than of Pope to make out the connection, we must observe that Lord Guildford's testimony, if ever given at all, is simply negative; he had found no proofs of the connection, but he had not found any proofs to destroy it; whilst, on the other hand, it ought to be mentioned, though unaccountably overlooked by all previous biographers, that one of Pope's anonymous enemies, who hated him personally, but was apparently master of his family history, and too honourable to belie his own convictions, expressly affirms, of his own authority, and without reference to any claim put forward by Pope, that he was descended from a junior branch of the Downe family; which testimony has a double value—first, as corroborating the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of Pope's statement viewed in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a fact; and, secondly, as corroborating that same statement viewed in the light of a current story, true or false, and not as a disingenuous fiction put forward by Pope to confute Lord Hervey. [Sir Thomas Pope, the founder of the Downe family, was of humble origin, the son of a yeoman at Deddington in Oxfordshire. He was enriched by the spoils of the church at the period of the Reformation, but died without issue. His brother was raised to the peerage in 1638. If, therefore, the poet's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were allied to this family, it must have been long before the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the peerage, through the Deddington yeoman.] It is probable to us that the Popes, who had been originally transplanted from England to Ireland, had, in the person of some cadets, been re-transplanted to England; and that having in that way been disconnected from all personal recognition, and all local memorials of the capital <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, by this sort of postliminium, the junior branch had ceased to cherish the honour of a descent which was now divided from all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> advantage. At all events, the researches of Pope's biographers have not been able to trace him farther back in the paternal line than to the grandfather; and he (which is odd enough, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> of his descendants), was a clergyman of the Established Church in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. This grandfather had two sons: of the eldest nothing is recorded beyond the three facts, that he went to Oxford, that he died there, and that he spent the family estate. The younger son, whose name was Alexander, had been sent when young, in some commercial character, to Lisbon; and there it was, in that centre of bigotry, that he became a sincere and most disinterested Catholic. He returned to England; married a Catholic young widow; and became the father of a second Alexander Pope, ultra Saurumatis notus et Antipodes. [The maternal ancestry of the poet has been minutely traced by the eminent archaeologist Mr Joseph Hunter, and by Mr Robert Davies of York. Edith Turner was not a widow when she married Alexander Pope. She was born at Worborough Dale, Yorkshire, and baptized June 15, 1642. She would thus seem to have been of the same age as her husband, both being in their fortieth year at the date of the poet's birth. The Turners were a family of 40 acres of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> and a small plantation in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of York. The poet's grandfather, William Turner, inherited from his uncle the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Towthorpe, lands in Ruston, with a rent-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of £70 on the manor of Ruston, and houses in the city of York. The rent-charge of £70 formed part of the dowry of Edith Turner, the last survivor of the family of fourteen children; and on the death of both his parents, it descended to the poet. William Turner died at York in 1665, his widow in 1681. "When upon the death of Mrs Turner," says Mr Davies, "the daughters who had remained under the maternal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> at York had to seek a home with married <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> in other parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, in whom Edith's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> to remove to London, where she became the wife of Alexander Pope, and the mother of the poet." One of the sisters was married to Samuel <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COOPER">Cooper</a>, the celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>-painter. Mrs Cooper was the poet's godmother, and by her will she left her godson, then only five years of age, her "painted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">china</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> with a silver foot and a dish to set it in;" and after her sister Elizabeth Turner's decease, all her books, pictures, and medals. Of the "sequestration and forfeitures of the family," mentioned by Pope, no trace has been found; and of three brothers, one, William, was the sole survivor in 1666. These children may have been connected with the poet's paternal ancestry. It has been found, however, that at the proper period, from 1631 to 1645, there was a Hampshire clergyman of the name of Alexander Pope. He had the rectory of Thruxton, and two other livings; but as there is no memorial of him in the church, and no entry in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of his having had children, it is still doubtful whether this rector of Thruxton was the poet's grandfather. The name was by no means an uncommon one.] By his own account to Spence, Pope learned "very early to read;" and writing he taught himself "by copying from printed books;" all which seems to argue that, as an only child, with an indolent father and a most indulgent mother, he was not molested with much schooling in his infancy. Only one adventure is recorded of his childhood,—viz., that he was attacked by a cow, thrown down, and wounded in the throat. Pope escaped this disagreeable kind of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VACCINATION">vaccination</a> without serious injury, and was not farther tormented by cows or schoolmasters until he was about eight years old, when the family priest,—that is, we presume, the confessor of his parents,—taught him, agreeably to the Jesuit system, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of Greek and Latin concurrently. This priest was named Banister; and his name is frequently employed, together with other fictitious names, by way of signature to the notes in the Dunciad, an artifice which was adopted for the sake of giving a characteristic variety to the notes, according to the tone required for the illustration of the text. From his tuition Pope was at length dismissed to a Catholic school at Twyford, near <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>. The selection of a school in this neighbourhood, though certainly the choice of a Catholic family was much limited, points apparently to the old Hampshire connection of his father. Here an incident occurred which most powerfully illustrates the original and constitutional determination to satire of this irritable poet. He knew himself so accurately that, in after times, half by way of boast, half of confession, he says,— " But touch me, and no Minister so sore: Who'er offends, at some unlucky time Slides into verse, and hitches in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a>, Sacred to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> his whole life long; And the sad burthen of some merry song." Already, it seems, in childhood he had the same irresistible <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, victorious over the strongest sense of personal danger. He wrote a bitter satire upon the presiding pedagogue, was brutally punished for this youthful indiscretion, and indignantly removed by his parents from the school. Mr Roscoe speaks of Pope's personal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> as necessarily unfavourable to public <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>; but in reality he knew nothing of public schools. All the establishments for Papists were narrow, and suited to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a>; and his parents were too sincerely anxious for their son's religious principles to risk the contagion of Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> by sending him elsewhere. From the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his disgrace and illiberal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, he passed, according to the received accounts, --- 1 It is apparently with allusion to this part of his history, which he would often have heard from the lips of his own father, that Pope glances at his uncle's memory somewhat disrespectfully in his prose letter to Lord Hervey. 2 Some accounts, however, say to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, in which case, perhaps, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> would have the honour of his conversion. 3 This however was not Twyford, according to an anonymous pamphleteer of the times, but a Catholic seminary in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> Street,— under the tuition of several other masters in rapid succession. But it is the less necessary to trouble the reader with their names, as Pope himself assures us that he learned nothing from any of them. To Banister he had been indebted for such trivial elements of a schoolboy's learning as he possessed at all, excepting those which he had taught himself. And upon himself it was, and his own admirable faculties, that he was now finally thrown for the rest of his education, at his age so immature that many boys are then first entering their academic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. Pope is supposed to have been scarcely twelve years old when he assumed the office of self-tuition, and bade farewell for ever to schools and tutors. Such a phenomenon is at any rate striking; it is the more so under the circumstances which attended the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and under the results which justified its execution. It seems, as regards the plan, hardly less strange that prudent parents should have acquiesced in a scheme of so much peril to his intellectual interests, than that the son, as regards the execution, should have justified their confidence by his final success. More especially this confidence surprises us in the father. A doubting mother might shut her eyes to all remote evils in the present gratification to her affections; but Pope's father was a man of sense and principle; he must have weighed the risks besetting a boy left to his own intellectual guidance; and to these risks he would allow the more <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> from his own conscious defect of scholarship and inability to guide or even to accompany his son's studies. He could neither direct the proper choice of studies, nor in any one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> taken separately could he suggest the proper choice of books. The case we apprehend to have been this: Alexander Pope the elder was a man of philosophical desires and unambitious character. Quiet and seclusion and innocence of life,—these were what he affected for himself; and that which had been found available for his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, he might reasonably wish for his son. The two hinges upon which his plans may be supposed to have turned were, first, the political <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECT">sect</a>; and, secondly, the fact that his son was an only child. Had he been a Protestant, or had he, though a Papist, been burdened with a large family of children, he would doubtless have pursued a different course. But to him, and, as he sincerely hoped, to his son, the strife after civil honours was sternly barred. Apostacy only could lay it open. And, as the sentiments of honour and duty in this point fell in with the vices of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> principle concurring with his constitutional <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of ease, we need not wonder that he should early retire from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with a very moderate competence, or that he should suppose the same fortune sufficient for one who was to stand in the same position. The son was from his birth deformed. That made it probable that he might not marry. If he should, and happened to have children, a small family would find an adequate provision in the patrimonial funds; and a large one at the worst could only throw him upon the same commercial exertions to which he had been obliged himself. The Roman Catholics, indeed, were just then situated as our modern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a> are: <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the one, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> to the other, closed all modes of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> employment except that of commercial industry. Either his son, therefore, would be a rustic recluse, or, like himself, he would be a merchant. With such prospects, what need of an elaborate education? And where was such an education to be sought? At the petty establishments of the suffering Catholics, the instruction, as he had found experimentally, was <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. At the great national establishments his son would be a degraded person; one who was permanently repelled from every arena of honour, and sometimes, as in cases of public danger, was banished from the capital, deprived of his house, left defenceless against common ruffians, and rendered liable to the control of every village <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. To one in these circumstances solitude was the wisest position; and the best qualification for that was an education that would furnish aids to solitary thought. No need for brilliant accomplishments to him who must never display them; forensic arts, pulpit erudition, senatorial eloquence, academical accomplishments,—these would be lost to one against whom the courts, the pulpit, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, were closed. Nay, by possibility worse than lost; they might prove so many snares or positive bribes to apostacy. Plain English, therefore, and the high thinking of his compatriot authors, might prove the best provision for the mind of an English Papist destined to seclusion. Such are the considerations under which we read and that is, in the Bloomsbury district of London; and the same author asserts that the scene of his disgrace, as indeed seems probable beforehand, was not the first but the last of his arenas as a schoolboy. Which indeed was first, and which last, is very unimportant; but with a view to another point, which is not without interest, namely, as to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of Pope for so bitter a lampoon as we must suppose it to have been, as well as with regard to the topics which he used to season it, this anonymous letter throws the only light which has been offered; and strange it is that no biographer of Pope should have hunted upon the traces indicated by him. Any solution of Pope's virulence, and of the master's bitter retaliation, even as a satire, is so far entitled to attention; apart from which the mere straightforwardness of this man's story, and its minute circumstantiality, weigh greatly in its favour. To our thinking he unfolds the whole affair in such simple exposition, nowhere else to be found, that the master of the school, the mean avenger of a childish insult by a brutal punishment, Mr Bromley, the uncle of James II.'s Popish apostates; whilst the particular statements which he makes with respect to himself and the young <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, 1760, as two schoolfellows of Pope at that time and place, together with his voluntary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to come forward in person, and verify his statement (if it be true), happen to be challenges which are, as we repeat, so many presumptions in favour of his veracity. "Mr Alexander Pope," says he, "better he had been four months at this school, or, if he had been employed in satirizing his master. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> of at least one hundred verses, which (a fellow-student having given information of it) was found in his pocket; and the young satirist was soundly whipped, and kept a prisoner in his room for seven days; whereupon his father fetched him away, and I have been told he never went to school more." This Bromley, it has been ascertained, was the son of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> gentleman in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, and must have had considerable prospects at one time, since it appears that he had been a gentleman-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> at Christ's Church, Oxford. There is an error in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PUNCTUATION">punctuation</a> of the letter which we have quoted; but affects the sense in a way very important to the question before us. Bromley is described as "one of King James's connects in Oxford, five years after that prince's abdication;" but if this were really so, he must have been a conscientious convert. The latter clause should be connected with what follows:—"Some years after that prince's abdication he kept a little seminary;" that is, when his mercenary views in quitting his religion were effectually defeated, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a> had sealed his despair, he had himself into a petty schoolmaster. These facts are interesting, because they suggest once more the merciless punishment inflicted upon Pope. His own father was a Papist like Bromley, but a sincere and honest Papist; who had borne the double legal stigmas, and public hatred for conscience sake. His contempt was habitually pointed at those who tampered with religion for interested purposes. His son inherited these upright feelings. And we may easily guess what would be the bitter sting of any satire he would write on Bromley. Such a topic was too true to be forgiven, and too keenly barbed by Bromley's conscience. By the way, this writer, like ourselves, reads in this juvenile adventure a prefiguration of Pope's satirical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>. [The statement referred to (signed "E. P.") and published by Curll) is likely to have been one of Pope's stratagems to mislead Curll, and keep up the public interest in his own personal history.] interpret the conduct of Pope's parents; and they <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to regard as wise and conscientious a scheme which, under ordinary circumstances, would have been pitifully foolish. And be it remembered, that to these considerations, derived exclusively from the civil circumstances of the family, were superadded others derived from the astonishing prematurity of the individual. That boy who could write at twelve years of age the beautiful and touching stanzas on Solitude, might well be trusted with the superintendence of his own studies. And the stripling of sixteen, who could so far transcend in good sense the accomplished statesmen or men of the world with whom he afterwards corresponded, might challenge confidence for such a choice of books as would best promote the development of his own faculties. In reality, one so finely endowed as Alexander Pope could not easily lose his way in the most extensive or ill-digested library. And though he tells Atterbury that at one time he abused his opportunities by reading controversial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, we may be sure that his own native activities, and the elasticity of his mind, would speedily recoil into a just equilibrium of study, under wider and happier opportunities. Reading, indeed, for a person like Pope, is rather valuable as a means of exciting his own energies, and of feeding his own sensibilities, than for any direct acquisitions of knowledge, or for any trains of systematic research. All men are destined to devour much rubbish between the cradle and the grave; and doubtless the man who is wisest in the choice of his books will have read many a page before he dies, that a thoughtful review would pronounce worthless. This is the fate of all men. But the reading of Pope, as a general result or measure of his judicious choice, is best justified in his writings. They show him well furnished with whatsoever he wanted for matter or for embellishment, or argument or illustration, for example and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, or for direct and explicit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. Possibly, as we have already suggested, within the range of English literature Pope might have found all that he wanted. But variety the widest has its uses; and, for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of his influence with the polished classes amongst whom he lived, he did wisely to add other languages; and a question has thus arisen with regard to the extent of Pope's attainments as a self-taught linguist. A man, or even a boy, of great originality, may happen to succeed best in working his own native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of thought, by his unassisted energies; here it is granted that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>, a guide, or even a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, may be dispensed with, and even beneficially. But in the case of foreign languages, in attaining this machinery of literature, though anomalies even here do arise, and men there are, like Joseph Scaliger, who form their own dictionaries and grammars in the mere <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of reading an unknown <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, by far the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> part of students will lose their time by rejecting the aid of tutors. As there has been much difference of opinion with regard to Pope's skill in languages, we shall briefly collate and bring into one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> the stray notices. As to the French, Voltaire, who knew Pope personally, declared that he "could hardly read it, and spoke not one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> of the language." But perhaps Voltaire might dislike Pope? On the contrary, he was acquainted with his works, and admired them to the very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of their merits. Speaking of him after death to Frederick of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, he prefers him to Horace and Boileau, asserting that, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with them, This is not a wise account of Pope, for it does not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> the characteristic feature of his power; but it is a very kind one. And of course Voltaire could not have meant any unkindness in denying his knowledge of French. But he was certainly wrong. Pope, in his presence, would decline to speak or to read a language of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> was confessedly beyond him. Or, if he did, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> left would be still worse. In fact, no man ever will pronounce or talk a language which he does not use, for some part of every day, in the real intercourse of life. But that Pope read French of an ordinary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> with fluency enough, is evident from the extensive use which he made of Madame Dacier's labours on the Iliad, and still more of La Valterie's prose translation of the Iliad. Already in the year 1718, and long before his personal knowledge of Voltaire, Pope had shown his accurate acquaintance with some voluminous French authors in a way which, we suspect, was equally surprising and offensive to his noble correspondent. The Duke of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> had addressed to Pope a letter containing some account of the controversy about Homer which had then been recently carried on in France between La Motie and Madame Dacier. This account was delivered with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> of teaching which was very little in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> with its excessive shallowness. Pope, who sustained the part of pupil in this interlude, replied in a manner that exhibited a knowledge of the parties concerned in the controversy much superior to that of the duke. In particular, he characterized the excellent notes upon Horace of M. Dacier the husband in very just terms, as distinguished from those of his conceited and half-learned wife; and the whole reply of Pope seems very much as though he had been playing off a mystification on his grace. Undoubtedly the pompous duke felt that he had caught a Tartar. Now, M. Dacier's Horace, which, with the text, fills nine volumes, Pope could not have read except in French; for they are not even yet translated into English. Besides, Pope read critically the French translation of his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Man, Essay on Criticism, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RAPE">Rape</a> of the Lock, &c. He spoke of them as a critic; and it was at no time a fault of Pope's to make false pretensions. All readers of Pope's Satires must also recollect numerous proofs that he had read Boileau with so much feeling of his peculiar merit that he has appropriated and naturalized in English some of his best <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>. Voltaire was therefore certainly wrong. Of Italian literature, meantime, Pope knew little or nothing; and simply because he knew nothing of the language. Tasso, indeed, he admired; and, which is singular, more than Ariosto. But we believe that he had read him only in English; and it is certain that he could not take up an Italian author, either in prose or verse, for the unaffected amusement of his leisure. Greek, we all know, has been denied to Pope, ever since he translated Homer, and chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of that translation. This seems at first sight unfair, because criticism has not succeeded in fixing upon Pope any errors of ignorance. His deviations from Homer were uniformly the result of imperfect sympathy with the naked simplicity --- 1 That is, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>, and legally speaking, of Buckinghamshire, there was lurking somewhere or other a claim to that title amongst the connections of the Villiers family. He was a pompous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANDEE">grandee</a>, who lived in uneasy splendour, and, as a writer, most extravagantly overrated; accordingly he is now forgotten. Such was his vanity, and his ridiculous mania for allying himself with royalty, that he first of all had the presumption to court the Princess (afterwards Queen <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>). Being rejected, he then offered himself to the illegitimate daughter of James II., by the daughter of Sir Charles Sedley. She was as ostentatious as himself, and accepted him. of the antique, and therefore wilful deviations, not (like those of his more pretending competitors, Addison and Tickell) pure blunders of misapprehension. But yet it is not inconsistent with this concession to Pope's merits, that we must avow our <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in his thorough ignorance of Greek when he first commenced his task. And to us it seems astonishing that nobody should have adverted to that fact as a sufficient solution, and in fact the only plausible solution, of Pope's excessive depression of spirits in the earliest stage of his labours. This depression, after he had once pledged himself to his subscribers for the fulfilment of his task, arose from, and could have arisen from nothing else, than his conscious ignorance of Greek in connection with the solemn responsibilities he had assumed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Nay, even countries as presumptuously disdainful of transmontane literature as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> took an interest in this memorable undertaking. Bishop Berkeley found Salvini reading it at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>; and Madame Dacier even, who read little but Greek, and certainly no English until then, condescended to study it. Pope's dejection, therefore, or rather agitation (for it impressed by sympathy a tumultuous character upon his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> which lasted for years after the cause had ceased to operate) was perfectly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> under the explanation we have given, but not otherwise. And how did he surmount this unhappy self-distrust? Paradoxical as it may <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, we will venture to say that, with the innumerable aids for interpreting Homer which even then existed, a man sufficiently acquainted with Latin might make a translation even critically exact. This Pope was not long in discovering. Other alleviations of his labour concurred, and in a ratio daily increasing. The same formulae were continually recurring, such as, "But him answering, thus addressed the swift-footed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>," Or, "But him eternally beholding, thus spoke Agamemnon the king of men." Then, again, universally the Homeric Greek, from many causes, is easy; and especially from these two: 1st, The simplicity of the thought, which never gathers into those perplexed knots of rhetorical condensation which we find in the dramatic poets of a higher civilization; 2dly, From the constant bounds set to the expansion of the thought by the form of the metre; an advantage of verse which makes the poets so much easier to a beginner in the German language than the illimitable weavers of prose. The line or the stanza reins up the poet tightly to his theme, and will not suffer him to expatiate. Gradually, therefore, Pope came to read the Homeric Greek, but never accurately; nor did he ever read Enstatius without aid from Latin. As to any knowledge of the Attic Greek, of the Greek of the dramatists, the Greek of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, the Greek of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, Pope neither had it nor affected to have it. Indeed it was no folly of Pope's, as we will repeat, to make claims which he had not, or even to dwell ostentatiously upon those which he had. And with respect to Greek in particular, there is a manuscript letter in existence from Pope to a Mr Bridges at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a> which, speaking of the original Homer, distinctly records the knowledge which he had of his own "imperfectness in the language." Chapman, a most spirited translator of Homer, probably had no very critical skill in Greek; and Hobbes was, beyond all question, as poor a Grecian as he was a doggerel translator; yet in this letter Pope professes his willing submission to the "authority" of Chapman and Hobbes as superior to his own. Finally, in Latin Pope was a "considerable proficient," even by the cautious testimony of Dr Johnson; and in this language only the doctor was an accomplished critic. If Pope had really the proficiency here ascribed to him, he must have had it already in his boyish years; for the translation from Statius, which is the principal monument of his skill, was executed before he was fourteen. We have taken the trouble to throw a hasty glance over it; and whilst we readily admit the extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> which it shows, as do all the juvenile essays of Pope, we cannot allow that it argues any accurate skill in Latin. The word Maléa, as we have seen noticed by some editor, he makes Maléa; which in itself, as the name was not of common occurrence, would not have been an error worth noticing; but, taken in connection with the certainty that Pope had the original line before him— "Arripit ex templo Malæa de valle resurgens," when not merely the scanning theoretically, but the whole rhythmus practically, to the most obtuse <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, would be annihilated by Pope's false <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, is a blunder which serves to show his utter ignorance of prosody. But, even as a version of the sense, with every allowance for a poet's license of compression and expansion, Pope's translation is defective, and argues an occasional inability to construe the text.
