RAMUS

Pages 816-817

PETRUS, the Latinized form of the name Pierre de la Ramee, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> celebrated alike by the persecutions of which he was made the object, and by the reforms which he endeavoured to introduce into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, science, and public instruction, was born at the little village of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTH">Cuth</a> in Picardy in 1515. His father, Jacques de la Ramee, pursued the humble occupation of a field labourer, but could <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> back his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> in a few removes to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. The boy lost his father at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and it was reserved for his mother, Jeanne Charpentier, to nurse him in poverty, and teach his young <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> early to handle the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of toil. Thrift and want combined early to develop his mind; and when only eight years old, we are told of his visiting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> all alone in pursuit of food and knowledge. Misery pursued the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> child there also, and he was compelled to retrace his steps. Again and again he visited the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> at short intervals, when his maternal uncle, struck with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perseverance, afforded him temporary shelter. Honoré Charpentier, who pursued the carpenter's craft, could not do more than allow him fairly to commence his studies. Ramus, who had now reached his twelfth year, was endowed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with a singularly robust <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and entered the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Navarre in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>. In this position he spent the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in his masters' <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and the night was devoted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. He attended the public course given by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">Faculty</a> of Arts in 1527, when he left it greatly in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with logic, and with a profound aversion for the manner in which it was taught. The first occasion on which Ramus expressed publicly his dissent from the logic of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> was at his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> for his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. This occurred in 1536, when Ramus had reached his twenty-first year. He chose for his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> the startling <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>, Quaecumque <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> Aristotele dicta esse, commenticia esse (All that has been affirmed by Aristotle is a fabrication). A subject so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> placed the judges in the very greatest embarrassment. "The master said it," was no guarantee to Ramus of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of a single proposition; and it was entirely in vain that all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIPATETICS">peripatetics</a> which Paris contained, united their influence to crush him. The young candidate urged his replies with so much spirit and vivacity, he managed his objections with so much subtlety, and sent them home with so much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, that all Paris was filled with astonishment and admiration. His admission to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of Master of Arts was a real triumph. Having thus enthusiastically won the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of instructing in the liberal arts, Ramus, in conjunction with Omer Talon, an able professor of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and Barthélémy Alexandre, a distinguished Greek scholar, established themselves in the little college of Ave-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a>. When in his twenty-eighth year Ramus published two books in Latin, of which even <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger condescended to extol the style. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the one was Dialecticae partitio <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> Academiam parisiensem; of the other, Aristotelice Anuadversiones,—the latter of which in particular subjected its author to incredible persecutions. Hardly had these two books seen the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> when the university, by its rector, Pierre Galland, solicited and obtained from the magistrates an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> for their immediate suppression. Their author was represented as an enemy to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and to the public peace. After endless jargonism, François I. resolved to bring this quarrel to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. A chairman and four judges, two of them selected by each party, were to sit in judgment between Ramus and his opponents. The upshot of it was, that Ramus was condemned, on the 1st <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1544, as having "acted rashly, arrogantly, and impudently." He was compelled to leave Paris, and he took up his residence at the college of Presles, where a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of students had taken refuge from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, and commenced a course of lectures on rhetoric. He returned to Paris in 1545, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> having been cancelled through the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of Lorraine. He began a course of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, which he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till 1551, when Henry II. appointed him professor of philosophy and eloquence in the College of France. The years which followed were the most tranquil of Ramus's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He wrote a Greek, a Latin, and a French <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, several treatises on mathematics, logic, and rhetoric. In 1551 Ramus embraced Protestantism, and his logical ardour, as it was said, compelled him to make an invasion into the domain of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. "Dès ce moment," adds a French biographer, "il fut perdu." Lost <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> not, Ramus had to flee the halter in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1562, and found an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Fontainebleau, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX. The royal protection was not sufficient for his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, for while absent his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was pillaged and his library destroyed. After the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBOISE">Amboise</a> in 1563 he resumed his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the capital, but did not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy it. Civil troubles in Paris induced him in 1568 to ask permission to travel. He visited a great many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, where "the French <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>" (Gallicus Plato) was received with much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. He resided for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in Bâle, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>, and taught his logic to the citizens of the three last-mentioned towns. Ramus had found it necessary, during his residence in Paris, strongly to oppose the appointment of one Jacques Charpentier to the mathematical chair of the university, from his profound, yea his avowed, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the subject. This person never forgave him. On his return to Paris, Ramus fell a victim to Charpentier's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> during the massacre of St. Bartholomew in 1572. Although Ramus had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> sufficient to overthrow the logic of Aristotle as it was then understood and interpreted, he was unfortunately incapable of raising anything better in its stead. He freed logic from the scholastic subtleties to which it was then applied, but forgot, in re-applying it, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> limits once and for all. He was not, in short, a profound thinker; he dealt more in rhetoric than in logic. Yet in freeing men's minds from the tyranny of a system he took a decided step in advance of his age, and deserves the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> for so doing. The system of Ramus speedily extended from France to Switzerland, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and Scotland, and was publicly taught in each of those countries. He left a great number of works, of which a detailed catalogue <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found in De Petri Rami Vita, Scriptis, Philosophia, by Waddington Kastus, Svo, Paris, 1818. Many of the author's works were translated into English and other foreign languages. The partizans of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> are known by the name of Ramists or Rameans.

RAMUSIO

Pages 817-817

Giambattista, an Italian who was born at Treviso in the Venetian State in 1485, began in the former half of the sixteenth century to edit a collection of the most notable voyages both <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. The circumstances of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> peculiarly qualified him for such a task. He had travelled in the character of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> through France, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. His acquaintance with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, and languages was <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. Many learned foreigners likewise were his friends and correspondents, and could communicate any information he might require. Thus aided, he carried on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> with success. Those parts of his collection which were written in foreign languages he translated into Italian. To those parts which were obscure <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> incorrect he added explanations and comments from the stock of his own knowledge. The first volume was published at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1550, under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Raccolta di Navigazioni e Viaggi; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> followed in 1556; and a third appeared in 1559, two years after the author's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

RANDERS

Pages 817-817

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>, on the navigable river Guden <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Gudelag, at the head of Randers Fiord, 22 miles N.N.W. of Aarhus, and 111 W.N.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. It occupies a position that is both very picturesque and strong in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> point of view; and it contains an arsenal, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. Much industry is carried on here, especially in the manufacture of hosiery and brandy. The trade is also considerable; and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> of salmon is pursued by many of the inhabitants. Pop. (1851) 7738.

RANDOLPH

Pages 817-818

Thomas, an English poet, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a> in 1605. He was educated at Westminster and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and was very early distinguished by his excellent genius. He gained the esteem and friendship of some of the greatest men of that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, particularly of Ben Jonson, who adopted him as one of his "sons." He has a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of fancy, and he writes melodious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; but his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> is bookish, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and gallantry is that of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> fellow and a reader of Ovid. He died under thirty in 1634. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are,—The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>' Looking-Glass, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMEDY">Comedy</a>; Auyatas, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the Impossible Dowry, a pastoral acted before the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>; Aristippus, or the Jovial <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">Philosopher</a>; The Conceited Pedlar; The Jealous Lover, a Comedy; Hey for Honesty, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with Knavery, a Comedy; and several other poems.

RANDOM SHOT

Pages 818-818

is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> made when the muzzle of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> is raised above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> line, and is not designed to shoot directly <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> point blank. The utmost randomness of any piece is about ten times as far as the bullet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> go point blank. The bullet will go farthest when the piece is mounted at an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of about 45° above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> range.

RANGE

Pages 818-818

the path of a bullet, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the line it describes from the mouth of the piece to the point where it lodges. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the piece <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a line <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, it is called the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> range; if it be mounted to 45°, it is said to have the utmost range; and all others between 6° and 45° are called the intermediate ranges. (See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUNNERY">GUNNERY</a>.)

RANGER

Pages 818-818

a sworn officer of a forest, appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>'s letters-patent, and whose proper business is to walk daily through his bailiwick, to drive back the deer out of the publick, and to present all trespasses within his jurisdiction at the next forest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>.

RANGOON

Pages 818-818

a seaport-town of British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Rangoon arm of the Irrawaddy, about 20 miles from its mouth, and 62 S. of Pegu. Previous to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fire which consumed the whole of the town in 1850, it occupied an <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> along the river's bank, about one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length and three-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> in breadth; but after that catastrophe it was rebuilt on a different site, about a mile from the river, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. It was built of bamboo for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, and defended by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAGODA">pagoda</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side, which formed a sort of citadel. In 1854 and 1855 fresh conflagrations took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the buildings they proved very destructive. In the re-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the town, since its last destruction, arrangements have been made by the British authorities for securing not only a proper protection against the recurrence of such devastations by fire, but for providing, by drainage and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and cleanliness of the town. The situation of Rangoon is very favourable to trade; and ship-building is actively carried on. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">Timber</a> is floated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the teak forests in the interior, and many vessels of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> size have been built here. The town was first built in 1753, by Alompra, the founder of the Burmese <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, and from him it derived its name, signifying the "<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">City</a> of Victory." It was taken by the British in the first Burmese <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> in 1824; but subsequently restored to the native power. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> war the capture of the pagoda <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> citadel by General Godwin in 1832 led to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the town; and it passed, along with the province of Pegu, into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the British. Pop., about 20,000. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">RANK</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">NAVY</a>, § Personnel.

RANK AND FILE

Pages 818-818

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> and vertical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> when drawn up for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. RANTERS. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">METHODISTS</a>.

RANZ DES VACHES

Pages 818-818

a simple and beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> which the Swiss herdsmen play on the Alpine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORN">horn</a> when driving out and in their herds to the pasture. Consisting, as it does, of a few simple intervals, the effect of it is quite enrapturing when heard among the echoes of the Swiss <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The native Swiss are said to be seized with inexpressible longings to return to their native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> when they hear it played in a foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>. This nostalgia <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> homesickness, as experienced by the Swiss soldier abroad, is elegantly alluded to by Rogers in his Pleasures of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">Memory</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> i., p. 19:— "The intrepid Swain, who guards a foreign shore, Condemned to climb his mountain-slope no more, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> chance he hears the song so sweet, so wild, His heart would <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> to hear it when a child, Melts at the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>-lost scenes that round him rise, And sinks a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to repentant sighs." (See Recherches sur les Ranz des Vaches, by Tarenne, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1813; Sammlung von Schweizer Kuhreigen und Volksliedern, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, 1818; also a Dissertatio de Nostalgia, by Th. Zwinger, Basle, 1710.)

RAOUL ROCHETTE

Pages 818-818

Désiré, an eminent French archaeologist, was born about 1789 at St. Amand, in the department of Cher, and received his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Bourget. His quick and facile talents soon began to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the world of letters. At the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty-two he was called to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the lycée at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. About four years afterwards he was translated to the same chair in the university of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Meanwhile he was commencing to prosecute the science of archaeology with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. The first result of his labours, published in 1815 under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Histoire Critique de l'Establishissement des Colonies Grecques, in 4 vols. 8vo, was favourably received by the public. This achievement stimulated him in his favourite investigations. It is true that a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was for a while directed to the topography and history of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. But he was soon found making frequent <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURS">tours</a> of discovery into different European countries, and perfecting his archaeological knowledge by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of museums and ruined buildings. A part of his researches appeared in 1822 under the title of Antiquités Grecques du Bosphore Cimmérien, and established his fame. So eminent, in fact, did he become, that he was appointed in 1826 to the chair of archaeology. The remainder of Raoul Rochette's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was occupied in maintaining that reputation which he had so laboriously gained. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make frequent incursions into the scenes of classical history, and to embody his discoveries in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of works. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> publications were,—Monuments Inédits d'Antiquité figurée Grecque, Étrusque, et Romaine, in folio, 1828; Pompeï : Choix d'Edifices Inédits, in folio, 1828; Peintures Antiques Inédites, in 4to, 1836; Mémoires de Numismatique et d'Antiquité, in 4to, 1840; and Mémoires d'Archéologie Comparée Asiatique, Grecque et Étrusque, in 4to, 1848. At his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1854, Raoul Rochette was perpetual secretary of the Academy of Fine Arts, and a corresponding member of most of the learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

RAPE

Pages 818-819

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the carnal knowledge of a woman forcibly and against her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a>. This, by the Jewish law, was punished with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> the damsel was betrothed to another <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and in case she was not betrothed, then a heavy fine of fifty shekels was to be paid to the damsel's father, and she was to be the wife of the ravisher all the days of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, without the power of divorce which was in general permitted by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic law</a>. The Roman law punishes with death and confiscation of goods the crime of ravishment, under which it includes both the offence of forcible <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABDUCTION">abduction</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> taking away a woman from her friends, and also the present one of forcibly dishonouring her; either of which, without the other, is in that law sufficient to constitute a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crime. The stealing away a woman from her parents or guardians, and debauching her, is equally penal by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s edict, whether she consent or be forced; and this in order to take away every opportunity of offending in this from women, whom the Roman law supposes never to go astray without the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SEDUCTION">seduction</a> and arts of the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and therefore, by restraining and making so highly penal the solicitations of the men, they meant to secure effectually the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the women. But our English law does not entertain quite such sublime <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the honour of either sex as to lay the blame of a mutual fault upon one of the transgressors only; and therefore it is a necessary ingredient in the crime of rape that it must be against the woman's will. Rape was punished by the Saxon laws, particularly those of Athelstan, with death; which was also agreeable to the old Gothic or Scandinavian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. But this was afterwards thought too hard; and in its stead another severe but not capital <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> was inflicted by William the Conqueror, namely, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CASTRATION">castration</a> and loss of eyes, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till after Bracton wrote, in the reign of Henry III. But in order to prevent malicious accusations, it was then the law that the woman should, immediately afterwards, go to the next town, and there make discovery to some credible persons, of the injury she had suffered, and afterwards should acquaint the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of the hundred, the coroners, and the sheriffs, with the outrage. This seems to correspond in some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> with the laws of Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, which require that complaint must be made within twenty-four hours; though afterwards by statute Westm. i., c. 13, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of limitation in England was extended to forty days. At present there is no time of limitation fixed; for, as it is usually now punished by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>, the maxim of law takes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that nullum tempus occurrit regi; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JURY">jury</a> will rarely give <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STALE">stale</a> complaint. During the former <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> also it was held for law, that the woman, by consent of the judge and her parents, might redeem the offender from the execution of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> by accepting him for her husband, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he also was willing to agree to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, but not otherwise. In the 3d Edward I., by the statute Westm. i., c. 13, the punishment of rape was much mitigated; the offence itself, of ravishing a damsel within <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that is, twelve years old, either with or without her consent, or of any other woman against her will, being reduced to trespass, if not prosecuted by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> within forty days, and subjecting the offender only to two years' imprisonment, and a fine at the king's will. But this lenity being productive of the worst consequences, it was, in ten years afterwards, 13 Edward I., found necessary to make the offence of forcible rape felony by statute Westm. ii., <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 34. And by statute 18 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, c.vii., it is made felony without benefit of clergy; as is also the abominable wickedness of carnally knowing or abusing any woman-child under the age of ten years, in which case the consent or non-consent is immaterial, as by reason of her tender years she is incapable of judgment and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Sir Matthew Hale is indeed of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that such profligate actions committed on an infant under the age of twelve years, the age of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> discretion by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, either with or without consent, amount to rape and felony, as well since as before the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Elizabeth. But that law has in general been held only to extend to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> under ten; though it should seem that damsels between ten and twelve are still under the protection of the statute Westm. i., the law with respect to their seduction not having been altered by either of the subsequent statutes. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> infant, under the age of fourteen years, is presumed by law to be incapable of committing a rape, and therefore, it seems, cannot be found guilty of it. For though in other felonies malitia supplet oculum; yet, as to this particular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of felony, the law supposes an imbecility of body as well as mind. The civil law seems to suppose a prostitute or common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARLOT">harlot</a>, incapable of any injuries of this kind; not allowing any punishment for violating the chastity of her who has indeed no chastity at all, or at least has no regard to it. But the law of England does not judge so hardly of offenders as to cut off all opportunity of retreat even from common strumpets, and to treat them as incapable of amendment. It therefore holds it to be felony to force even a concubine or harlot, because the woman may have forsaken that unlawful course of life; for, as Bracton well observes, licet meretricius fuerit antea, certe tunc temporis non fuit, cum reclamando negatique ejus consentire voluit. Capital punishment for this offence was abolished by 4 Vict. 1841, and transportation substituted.

RAPHOE

Pages 819-819

a market-town of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DONEGAL">Donegal</a>, in a beautiful situation, amid a rich and well-cultivated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, 3 miles N.W. of Lifford, and 135 N.N.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It contains a plain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUCIFORM">cruciform</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, formerly the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Raphoe, which is now united with that of Derry. There are also various dissenting places of worship, a free school, national school, and others; a neat market-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, library, dispensary, &c. In the vicinity are the deanery, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome edifice formerly the episcopal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. Pop. (1851) 1492.

RAPIN

Pages 819-819

PAUL DE, Seigneur de Thoyras, an eminent historian, was the son of Jacques de Rapin, and was born at Castres in 1661. He was first educated under a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in his father's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and was afterwards sent to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAMUR">Samur</a>. In 1679 he returned to his father, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to apply himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and was admitted an advocate; but reflecting that his being a Protestant would prevent his advancement at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he soon after resolved to quit the profession of the law, and to apply himself to that of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. His father, however, would not consent to the change. The revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, which happened two months afterwards, made him resolve to come to England; but as he had no hopes of any settlement there, his stay was but short. He therefore went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and enlisted himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of French volunteers at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, commanded by M. Rapin, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>-german. He attended the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> into England in 1688; and the following year <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> made him an ensign in his regiment, with which he proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where he gained the esteem of his officers at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARRICKFERGUS">Carrickfergus</a>, and soon received a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. He was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>, and was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> through the shoulder at the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>. He was soon afterwards made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the company in which he had been ensign; but in 1693 he resigned his company to one of his brothers, in order to become tutor to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Portland's son. Having finished this employment, he returned to his family, which he had settled at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some years. But as he found his family increase, he resolved to retire to some cheap <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and accordingly removed in 1707 to Wesel, where he commenced his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England. Though he was of a strong <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, yet seventeen years' application entirely ruined his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. He died in 1725. Rapin wrote in French a Dissertation sur les Whigs et les Tories. His Histoire d'Angleterre was printed at the Hague in 1726 and 1727, in 9 vols. 4to, and reprinted at Trevoux in 1728, in 10 vols. 4to. This last edition is more complete than that of the Hague. It has been translated into English, and improved, with notes by Tindal, in 2 vols. folio, 1737–39. This performance, although the work of a foreigner, is deservedly esteemed as one of the fullest and most impartial collections of English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> transactions extant.

RASCOVA

Pages 821-821

RASCOVA, a fortified town of European Turkey, on the right bank of the Danube, at the place where that river turns suddenly to the north, 38 miles E. by N. of Sinistra. Near this begins the line of earth-works called Trajan's Wall, stretching across the isthmus of Dobrudschka to the Black Sea. Rasova was occupied by the Russians for a short time in 1854. Pop. 8000.

RASGRAD

Pages 819-819
or HESAROAD, a town of European Turkey, in Bulgaria, in a lofty position overlooking a ravine, on the Ak or White Lern, an affluent of the Danube, 215 miles N.W. of Constantinople. It is a place of considerable trade, standing at the junction of four main roads. Strong in its natural position, it is further defended by a dry ditch and palisade. The Turks were defeated here by the Russians in 1810. Pop. 16,000.

RASK

Pages 819-820

Rasmus Christian, an eminent scholar and philologist, was born at Brendekilde, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> of Fyen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNEN">Funen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in 1787. He studied at the uni- versity of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, and early distinguished himself by singular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for the acquisition of languages. In the year 1808 he was appointed assistant-keeper of the university library, and some years afterwards made professor of literary <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. In 1811 he published, in the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, his *Introduction to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a> of the Icelandic and other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Northern Languages*, the materials of which were entirely derived from the immense <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of manuscript and printed works which had been accumulated by his predecessors in the same field of research. This grammar appears to have given a fresh impulse to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the ancient northern languages, even in Germany. The reputation which Rask acquired by it recommended him to the Arnamagnæan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">Institution</a>, by which he was employed as editor of the Icelandic *Lexicon* of Bjorn Haldorsen, which had <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> remained in manuscript. To this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which appeared in 1814, Bishop Müller contributed a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, in which he pronounces a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> eulogium on the talents and the spirit of research displayed by the youthful editor. About the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, Rask who had never been in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, paid a visit to that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where he remained from 1813 to 1815, during which time he made himself completely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the language, and familiarized himself with the literature, manners, and customs of the natives. To the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with which they inspired him may probably be attributed the establishment at Copenhagen, early in 1816, of the Icelandic Literary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, which was mainly instituted by his exertions, and of which he had the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. Whilst thus employed, however, he was about to enter upon a more ample field of enterprise. In October 1816 he left Denmark on a literary expedition, which had been fitted out for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> purpose of prosecuting inquiries into the languages of the East, and collecting <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> for the University Library at Copenhagen. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> of Denmark having liberally provided him with the requisite means, he proceeded first to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, where he remained two years, in the course of which he made an excursion into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, for the purpose of studying the language of that country. Here he published, in Swedish, his *Anglo-Saxon Grammar* in 1817; and during the same year there appeared at Copenhagen, in Danish, an *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Origin of the Ancient Scandinavian or Icelandic Tongue*, in which he traced the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> of that remarkable idiom to the other European languages, particularly to the Latin and the Greek. In 1818 he published a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition, very much improved, of his *Icelandic Grammar*, translated by himself into Swedish; and in the course of the same year he also brought out the first complete editions of Snorror's *Edda*, and Sæmundr's *Edda*, in the original text, along with Swedish translations of both *Eddas*, the originals and the versions occupying each two volumes. From <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a> he proceeded in 1819 to St Petersburg, where he wrote in German an interesting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on "The Languages and Literature of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, Iceland, Sweden, and Finland," which was published in the sixth <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> *Jahrbücher*. From Russia, which he traversed, he proceeded through <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and resided for some time at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TAURIS">Tauris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TEHERAN">Teheran</a>, Persepolis, and Shiraz. It may be mentioned here, as an instance of his remarkable facility in acquiring languages, that in about six weeks he made himself sufficiently master of the Persian to be able to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> freely in that language with the natives. In 1820 he embarked at Abuscheik, in the Persian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, which he reached in safety; and during his residence there he wrote in English "A Dissertation on the Authenticity of the Zend Language," which he addressed to the governor, the Hon. Mounstuart Elphinstone, and which was afterwards published in the third volume of the *Transactions of the Literary Society of Bombay*. The same production, with corrections and additions, was afterwards deemed worthy of insertion in the *Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Asiatic Society*. From Bombay he proceeded through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> to Ceylon, where he arrived in 1822, and soon afterwards wrote, in English, "A Dissertation respecting the best Method of expressing the Sounds of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Languages in European <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">Characters</a>," which was printed in the *Transactions of the Literary and Agricultural Society of Colombo*. Professor Rask, having at length completed his researches on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> prescribed, set out for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and reached Copenhagen in the beginning of May 1823, after an absence of nearly <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. He brought home with him a considerable collection of rare and curious oriental manuscripts, Persian, Zend, Pali, Cingalese, and others, which now enrich the university and royal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> of the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Notwithstanding all his labours and exertions, this indefatigable scholar scarcely allowed himself an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of repose. Between the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his return from the East and that of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which occurred far too soon for the interests of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOLOGY">philology</a>, Professor Rask published in his native language a *Spanish Grammar* in 1824, an *Italian Grammar* and a *Frisic Grammar* in 1825, a *Treatise respecting the Ancient Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>* in 1827, the *Ancient Jewish Chronology previous to Moses* in 1828, and an *Essay on Danish Orthography* in the same year. He likewise edited an edition of Schneider's *Danish Grammar for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of Englishmen* in 1829, and superintended the English translation of his *Anglo-Saxon Grammar* by Thorpe in 1830. This last work supplies what had long been a desideratum in English literature. Before its appearance persons whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> might dispose them to investigate our early vernacular remains had no guides to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them, and each had to form for himself a grammar and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of the Saxon. Hickes' was full of blunders, and in these Elstob, Lye, Manning, and others had religiously followed him, superadding their own contingents respectively. Rask's services to comparative philology were very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. He was the first to point out the connection between the ancient Northern and Gothic on the one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and of the Lithuanian, Slavonic, Greek, and Latin on the other. In private <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the character of Professor Rask was such as to command admiration and respect. His manners, though somewhat retiring, were mild and gentle, and his morals unimpeachable. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of living was simple in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> almost that of an anchorite. The habits of study and application which he had acquired in his youth were never laid aside. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> he was diffident, and always expressed himself with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>; but when the subject involved anything relative to his own history or pursuits, he evinced a reluctance to converse which seemed to grow upon him with years, and almost amounted to a morbid <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. His facility in the acquisition of languages was extraordinary; he appeared to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a knowledge of them by a sort of intuition, and his mind seemed to recollect rather than to learn. In 1822 he was master of no less than twenty-five languages and dialects. His knowledge of English was extensive and correct. He spoke and wrote it with such fluency and precision that Englishmen to whom he was introduced were accustomed to ask him how long he had been in England, considering that such an acquaintance could only be gained by a residence in the country where it was spoken. Rask, in his personal appearance, was thin and spare, but well made; his habits of temperance, regularity, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, had contributed to give him all the appearance of a healthy <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and he seemed destined to attain a ripe old <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was capable of enduring much fatigue, and even the privation of necessary rest; changes of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> seemed to produce no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; the scorching <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> of India, and the biting frosts of Iceland, were equally braved and disregarded. But, with all this apparent superiority to ordinary infirmities, he

RASTADT, OR RASTALL

Pages 821-821

RASTADT, or RASTALL, a fortified town of the grand duchy of Baden, circle of Middle Rhine, on the Murg, not far from its confluence with the Rhine, 14 miles S. of Carlsruhe, and 30 N.E. of Strasburg. The palace, formerly occupied by the margraves of Baden-Baden, a building four storeys high, after the model of the palace at Versailles, is the most conspicuous edifice. It stands on a height, and has a tower surmounted with a gilt statue of Jupiter, and commanding an extensive view. The town is regularly built, and has several churches, a lyceum, and a normal school. Manufactures of tobacco, snuff, cutlery, mathematical and musical instruments are carried on here; and there is a considerable trade. Rastadt was first brought into importance by the Margrave Louis William, who had fixed his residence here in the end of the seventeenth century, it having previously been but a small village. The peace of 1714, which put an end to the war of the Spanish succession, was signed in the palace by Prince Eugene and Marshal Villars. A congress was held here in 1797-9, to negotiate a peace between France and the empire, after which the French ambassadors, Roberjet and Bonnier, were murdered on their return, only a short distance from the town, but by whom it was never ascertained. A monument now marks the place. At Rastadt the insurrection in Baden in 1849 first broke out; and the insurgents, after a three weeks' siege, were obliged to surrender at discretion to the Prussians. Pop. 7284.

RASTALL, JOHN

Pages 821-821

RASTALL, John, a printer and miscellaneous writer, was born in London probably about the end of the fifteenth century, and educated at Oxford. Returning from the university, he settled in the metropolis and commenced printer, "then esteemed," says Wood, "a profession fit for any scholar or ingenious man." He married the sister of Sir Thomas More, with whom, we are told, he was very intimate, and whose writings he strenuously defended. From the title-page of one of his books, he appears to have lived in Cheapside, at the sign of the Mermaid. He died in the year 1536; and left two sons, William and John; the first of whom became a judge in Queen Mary's reign, and the other a justice of peace. The subject of the present article was a zealous Papist; but Bale says that he changed his religion before his death. He wrote *Natura naturata*, which Pitts calls a copious and ingenious comedy, describing Europe, Asia, and Africa. *The Pastyme of the People; the cronycles of diverse realayes, and most especially of the realm of England, brevily compiled and emprinted in Cheapeygde, at the sign of the Mermaid, next Pollysgate, cum privilegio, folio*. It was reprinted in 1811 in the *Collection of English Chronicles*. *Ecclesia Johannis Rastalli*, 1542, was one of the prohibited books in the reign of Henry VIII. He also wrote *Legum Anglicarum vocabula explicata*, French and Latin, London, 1567, 8vo.

RASTENBURG

Pages 821-821

RASTENBURG, a town of Prussia, in the province of Prussia, and circle of Königsberg, on the Gube, 55 miles S.E. of Königsberg. It is distinguished by the high, red roofs of the houses; and contains a castle, several churches, a gymnasium, &c. Linen is woven here, and forms the principal article of trade. Pop. 4805.

RATAFIA

Pages 821-821

RATAFIA, a fine spirituous liquor prepared from the kernels and other parts of several kinds of fruits, particularly cherries and apricots. Ratafia of cherries is prepared by bruising the cherries, and putting them into a vessel wherein brandy has long been kept; then adding to them the kernels of cherries, with strawberries, sugar, cinnamon, white pepper, nutmeg, cloves, and to twenty pounds of cherries ten quarts of brandy. The vessel is left open ten or twelve days, and then stopped close for two months before it is tapped. Ratafia of apricots is prepared in two ways,—namely, either by boiling the apricots in white wine, adding to the liquor an equal quantity of brandy, with sugar, cinnamon, mace, and the kernels of apricots, infusing the whole for eight or ten days, then straining the liquor, and putting it up for use; or by infusing the apricots, cut in pieces, in brandy for a day or two, passing it through a straining-bag, and then putting in the usual ingredients. The French excel in this species of distillation.

RATHANGAN

Pages 821-821

RATHANGAN, a market-town of Ireland, county of Kildare, on the Little Barrow, 5 miles N. by W. of Kildare, and 31 W.S.W. of Dublin. It is pretty well built, and contains a handsome parish church; various other places of worship, two schools, a dispensary, and several large flour-mills. There are hardly any manufactures or trade here. Pop. (1851) 1004.

RATHDOWNEY

Pages 821-821

RATHDOWNEY, a market-town of Ireland, Queen's County, on an affluent of the Nore, 19 miles S.W. of Maryborough. It has a good parish church, Methodist and Roman Catholic chapels, two schools, a barrack, and a dispensary. In the parish there are, besides other remains, those of an abbey and of three castles. A brewery and a boulting-mill are the only manufactories. Pop. (1851) 1192.

RATHENOW

Pages 821-821

RATHENOW, or Rathenau, a town of Prussia, in the province of Brandenburg and circle of Potsdam, on the Havel, 48 miles W. of Berlin. It contains a church with a newly-erected Gothic tower, a gymnasium, and a girls' school. There is also a monument and a statue of the elector Frederick-William. Among the manufactures, the most important is that of optical instruments; fishing, brewing, distilling, and navigation, give employment to many of the people. A victory was gained here in 1675 by the troops of Brandenburg over the Swedes. Pop. 6432.

RATHKEALE

Pages 821-821

RATHKEALE, a market-town of Ireland, county of Limerick, on the Deel, 16 miles S.W. of Limerick, and 136 S.W. by W. of Dublin. Many of the houses are well built; and there are a parish church, Roman Catholic and other places of worship, a court-house, jail, several schools, hospital, dispensary, and workhouse. The inhabitants are mostly employed in farming, and there is a considerable retail trade. The ruins of an old priory and of two castles are to be seen here. Rathkeale derived much advantage from a colony of German Protestants who settled here in the beginning of the eighteenth century. Pop. (1851) 3029.

RATIBOR

Pages 821-821

RATIBOR, a town of Prussia, in the province of Silesia and government of Oppeln, on the left bank of the Oder, 40 miles S.S.E. of Oppeln. It is walled, entered by four gates, and defended by a castle. There are here a court of appeal for Upper Silesia, several churches, a gymnasium, and other schools, several hospitals, &c. Manufactures and trade are actively carried on; and much-frequented markets are held for corn, cattle, wool, flax, and hemp. Pop. 9691.

RATION

RATION, a portion of ammunition, bread, drink, and forage, distributed to each soldier in an army for his daily subsistence. The horse have rations of hay and oats when they cannot go out to forage.

RATIONALISM

Pages 821-821

RATIONALISM, in its widest acceptation, is applicable to all who follow the dictates of reason, whether in their speculative or practical life. In its more restricted signification it is applied specially to that system of religious opinion whose final test of truth is placed in the direct assent of the human consciousness, whether in the form of logical deduction, moral judgment or religious intuition, by whatever previous process these facilities may have been raised to their assumed dignity as arbitrators. The rationalist, as such, is not bound to maintain that a divine revelation of religious truth is impossible, nor even to deny that it has actually been given. He may admit the fact of a revelation, and may accept certain portions of it as of permanent authority; but he assigns to the higher tribunal of his consciousness the right of determining what is essential to religion and what is not.

RATISBON

Pages 822-823

RATISBON (Germ. Regensburg, Fr. Ratisbonne), a town of Bavaria, in the upper palatinate, on the right bank of the Danube, here crossed by an ancient stone bridge, at its confluence with the Regen, 65 miles N.N.E. of Munich. It has an antique and somewhat dull appearance, as it has greatly fallen off from its former size and splendour. The old walls which surround it are in a dilapidated condition, and the ditches filled up. Entrance is obtained by six gates into the town, where the streets, narrow and crooked, though clean, are lined with old-fashioned stone buildings. Several loop-holed embattled towers rise from the houses to remind the spectators of the ancient turbulent times; and in the street of the ambassadors there are many memorials of the days when its splendid mansions were occupied by the representatives of great monarchs and nations. The arms of various countries decorate many of the houses, among which are the eagle of Austria and the lion of St Mark. The Gothic cathedral of St Peter, though both of its towers are unfinished, is one of the masterpieces of German architecture. It was begun in 1275, and left off in 1634. The ground plan is peculiar, as the lower storey has no transepts, but only the upper. The western front is extremely beautiful, and richly adorned. In the interior are many fine statues and works of art; among the rest, the high altar of solid silver. From the summit of the building a beautiful and extensive view is obtained over the course of the Danube, with the chain of the Alps in the distance. Within the cathedral inclosure are the remains of two more ancient churches, curious and interesting to the antiquarian. There are numerous other churches in the town, but few of them possess much interest. A gloomy and irregular old building near the cathedral is the town-hall, the meeting-place of the German Diets from 1663 till 1806. In the assembly-hall are still to be seen the seats and benches which are said to have been used. The building also contains dungeons and a torture chamber; in the latter, directly below the hall of the Diet, is the most perfectly preserved collection of instruments of cruelty that exists in Europe. A large building, formerly the Benedictine convent of St Emmeran, is now the residence of the Count of Thurn and Taxis. In the garden belonging to it stands a monument to Kepler, who died at Ratisbon in 1630, and is buried in the adjacent churchyard. The town contains, besides the buildings already mentioned, a theatre, public library, picture gallery, collection of antiquities; lyceum, gymnasium, and other schools; hospital, infirmary, orphan and blind asylums, &c. The manufactures include beer, brandy, tobacco, leather, wax-candles, porcelain, earthenware, paper, cotton, steel, brass, &c. Ship-building is actively carried on, and there is a considerable trade and navigation on the Danube; salt, timber, and corn, being the chief articles of commerce. In the vicinity of Ratisbon stands the Walhalla, a building after the model of the Parthenon at Athens, containing busts and monuments of celebrated Germans from the earliest period. It was founded by King Lewis of Bavaria in 1830, and completed in 1842; a magnificently-adorned building, but, as a temple of Fame, not by any means so impressive as the time-hallowed fane of other countries. It stands on a hill commanding towards the east, a view of the dark slopes of the Bavarian Forest on the north of the Danube, and the rich plain of Straubing on the south, with the ruin-crowned heights of Donaustauf, and the towers of Ratisbon to the west, and in clear weather the distant Alps to the south. Ratisbon is a town of great antiquity, and was a place of some importance under the Romans. With the exception of one square tower, said to be of Roman origin, there are no remains of this period. The first German emperor, Louis the German, fixed his residence here; and the town was afterwards the seat of the dukes of Bavaria, and the capital of that country. Frederick Barbarossa, in the twelfth century, made Ratisbon immediately dependent on the empire, and as such it remained till 1803, when it was given to the Archbishop of Mentz. The town enjoyed great prosperity during the middle ages; but, like Augsburg and Nuremberg, it fell into decay after the discovery of the Cape of Good Hope. In 1809 it passed again into the possession of Bavaria. Pop. 25,000.

RATLINES

Pages 823-823

RATLINES, or, as the sailors call them, ratlines, those lines which form the ladder-steps to the shrouds of a ship.

RATTANS

Pages 823-823

RATTANS, commercially rattan-canes, are the whip-like prolongations (flagelli) of the petioles of Calamus Roxburghii, Griffiths, the C. Rotang of Roxburgh and other species (Nat. Ord. Palmaeae). These flagelli are often of very great length, and as they are armed at their extremities with long sharp prickles, when pushed amongst the foliage of other trees they serve as tendrils to these climbing palms. The greater portion of the flagellum is smooth and glossy, with a thick silicious coating having the appearance of varnish, and being very indestructible. They are collected in Bengal, along the Coromandel coast, in Java, and in China, in vast quantities, and are used very extensively for a great variety of purposes in all parts of the peninsula of India, from which they are largely exported to all parts of the world. Their great strength and flexibility, their cylindrical form, the ease with which they split, &c., render them applicable to a variety of purposes. The Hindustanese make hats, shoes, chairs, bedsteads, baskets, sieves, and other useful articles of them. They likewise use them as ropes for binding their wooden houses together, and form a great variety of mats from them. The Chinese use them to a great extent instead of cord for tying round their tea-chests. In Europe they are chiefly used in forming the bottoms of chairs and stools, and as a cheap substitute for whalebone. The imports in 1858 were 8,901,600 rattans. They usually come in bundles of about fifty in each, the canes being about 16 feet in length, and once bent in the bundle.

RAUCH, CHRISTIAN

Pages 823-824

RAUCH, CHRISTIAN, one of the greatest sculptors of modern times, was born at Arolsen, in the principality of Waldeck, on the 2d of January 1777. The opening career of the young artist was attended with considerable difficulty. His parents were poor, and could not afford to place him under efficient masters. His first instructor, Valentin of Arolsen, taught him little else than the art of sculpturing grave-stones. Professor Ruhl of Cassel could not give him much more. A wider field of improvement opened up before him when he removed to Berlin in 1797; but poverty still hampered all his efforts. He was obliged to earn a livelihood by becoming a royal lacquerer, and to reserve the prosecution of his favourite art for his spare hours. The genius of Rauch, however, soon forced itself into notice, and recommended him to several influential individuals who were able to give him assistance. Queen Louisa surprising him one day in the act of modelling her fair features in wax, sent him to study at the Academy of Art. Not long afterwards, in 1804, Count Sandrecky gave him the means to go and complete his education at Rome. There also he found both aid and encouragement. William Von Humboldt directed his attention to the antique. Canova and Thorwaldsen advised and stimulated him in that study. Under such propitious patronage the young sculptor made rapid progress. Among other works, he executed bas-reliefs of "Hippolytus and Phaedra," "Mars and Venus wounded by Diomedes," and a "Child Praying." It was in 1811 that Rauch entered upon the eminent part of his career. Commissioned in that year to execute a monument for Queen Louisa of Prussia, he summoned up all his strength and industry for the arduous task. It is said that he shut himself up from all intercourse with the world until, by unwearied meditation and experiment, he had caught and embodied the features of his departed patroness. The statue, representing the queen in a sleeping posture, was placed in a mausoleum in the grounds of Charlottenburg, and procured great fame for the artist. Commissions for portraits came pouring in upon him. The consummate tact with which he seized individual characteristics, and the artistic manner in which he treated them, established at once his reputation. The erection of all public statues came to be entrusted to him. He began to execute that long series of representations of great Germans in which his genius is exhibited to full advantage. As years passed by, statesmen, patriots, and men of genius, some colossal and others of the ordinary size, continued to come forth from his studio. In course of time almost every important town throughout the country possessed a bust of some worthy fresh and vigorous from his matchless chisel. There were, among others, Blücher at Breslau, King Maximilian at Munich, Pastor Franke at Halle, Albert Dürer at Nuremberg, Luther at Wittenberg, and the Grand Duke Paul Frederick at Schwerin. At length he reached the climax of his efforts, by commencing in 1840 a colossal monument at Berlin to Frederick the Great. This work was inaugurated with great pomp, and in the presence of a vast assemblage, in May 1851, and has ever since been regarded as one of the grandest masterpieces of modern sculpture. On a granite pedestal 25 feet in height stands the colossal equestrian statue of the king. His plain, pinched features, and his grotesque costume, are given with historical exactness, without impairing the artistic effect. An air of resistless majesty emboldens the mean countenance, and a bold and skilful treatment hides the absurdity of the garb. Nor are the representations on the pedestal less correct or less successful. On each of the four faces designs in high relief, of the size of life, and executed after authentic portraits, busts, or medals, appear lively groups of the generals, statesmen, and great men of the reign. Beneath these figures are tablets bearing the names of other noted Prussian contemporaries. Above are female forms of Justice, Strength, Wisdom, and Moderation, interspersed with emblematic bas-reliefs of the principal periods of the monarch's career. In fact, the entire monument is a vivid history in stone of the life and reign of Frederick the Great. These numerous labours of Rauch were rewarded by a happy old age. The matchless excellence of his masterpiece had been recognised throughout the world, Princes decorated him with honours. All the academies of Europe enrolled him among their members. Especially did his own sovereign and countrymen regard him with proud affection and respect. Of late years his fine form, the very embodiment of elevated and venerable genius, was an object of interest at the court-balls of Berlin. Nor did he take less pleasure than he had ever done in the prosecution of his art. As he said himself, "his working-room was his home." A statue of Kant for Königsberg, and a statue of Thaer for Berlin, occupied his attention during some of his last years; and he had just finished a model of "Moses praying between Aaron and Hur," when the illness attacked him which eventually carried him off on the 3rd December 1857.

RAVALLIAC, OR RAVALLAC

Pages 824-824

RAVALLIAC, or RAVALLAC, François, the assassin of Henri IV., of France, was born at Angoulême about 1578, and was at the time of his execution about thirty-two years of age. Ravallac was the son of humble parents, his father being one of those inferior retainers of the law to whom the vulgar give the name of pettebloggers, a profession to which his son had also been bred. He taught a school for some time, and seems to have been imprisoned for debt, which greatly affected his mind. His distress was so great that he had much ado to live. When he was seized for the murder of the king, he was very loosely guarded, and all were permitted to speak with him who pleased. He was removed next day from the house of Espernon to the Conciergerie, the proper prison of the Parliament of Paris. When he was first interrogated, he answered with great boldness, that he had done it, and would do it if it were to be done again. When he was told that the king, though dangerously wounded, was living, and might recover, he said that he had struck him home, and that he was sure he was dead. He persisted in the most solemn asseverations that he had no accomplices, and that nobody had persuaded him to the fact. He appeared surprised at nothing so much as at the universal abhorrence of the people, which, it seems, he did not expect. When he was put to the torture, he broke out into horrid execrations, and always insisted that he did the act from his own motive, and that he could accuse nobody. On the day of his execution, after he had made the amende before the church of Notre Dame, he was carried to the Grève; and, being placed upon a scaffold, was tied to a wooden engine in the shape of St. Andrew's cross. The knife with which he did the murder being fastened in his right hand, it was first burned in a slow fire; then the fleshy parts of his body were torn with red-hot pincers, and melted lead, oil, pitch, and resin poured into the wounds. The people refused to pay for him; and when, according to the sentence that had been pronounced upon him, he came to be dragged to pieces by four horses, one of those that were brought appearing to be but weak, a spectator offered his own, with which the criminal was much moved. He was very earnest for absolution, which his confessor refused, unless he would reveal his accomplices. "Give it me," said he, "upon condition that I have told the truth;" which the priest eventually did. His body resisted the force of the horses; and the executioner cut him into quarters, which the people dragged through the streets. There has just been published Le Procès du tres Mechant et Detestable Parricide Francois Ravallac, by Auguste Aubry, Paris, 1859, compiled from the original MSS. of the trial.
